questions.raw_text: Explain why carbon forms covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds.

stem.text: Explain why carbon forms covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds.

topic_names: 4.1 BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: Carbon has four valence electrons and needs to gain or lose four electrons to attain a noble gas configuration. Losing four electrons requires high energy, and gaining four electrons is difficult due to nuclear instability. Hence, carbon shares electrons through covalent bonding to achieve stability.

questions.answer: Diamond is the hardest natural substance because each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid three-dimensional tetrahedral structure, forming strong covalent bonds throughout the crystal.

questions.raw_text: Explain the formation of a double covalent bond with an example.

stem.text: Explain the formation of a double covalent bond with an example.

topic_names: 4.1 BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons. For example, in an oxygen molecule (O₂), each oxygen atom has six valence electrons and needs two more electrons to complete its octet. Hence, each oxygen atom contributes two electrons, forming two shared pairs, which constitutes a double bond. This is represented as O=O. The double bond is stronger and shorter than a single bond, and results in a stable molecule.

questions.raw_text: Compare the bonding in methane (CH₄) and ammonia (NH₃), focusing on how each atom attains noble gas configuration.

stem.text: Compare the bonding in methane (CH₄) and ammonia (NH₃), focusing on how each atom attains noble gas configuration.

topic_names: 4.1 BONDING IN CARBON - THE COVALENT BOND
questions.answer: In methane (CH₄), carbon has four valence electrons and shares one electron with each of four hydrogen atoms, forming four single covalent bonds. This allows carbon to attain the electronic configuration of neon (octet) and each hydrogen to attain the configuration of helium (duplet). In ammonia (NH₃), nitrogen has five valence electrons and shares three electrons with three hydrogen atoms, forming three single covalent bonds. Nitrogen thus achieves an octet, and each hydrogen achieves a duplet. Both molecules achieve stability through covalent sharing without forming ions.
